description: The invasion triggered a major supply shock and a rapid repricing of geopolitical risk.
OPEC raised production targets ahead of weakening demand during the Asian financial crisis.
OPEC and major producers coordinated output cuts after a steep oil price decline.
The attacks intensified macro uncertainty and altered expectations for transport fuel demand.
The Iraq war increased uncertainty around Middle East supply and export continuity.
Lehman Brothers collapsed and recession fears drove a severe demand outlook revision.
Regional instability reshaped expectations for oil supply resilience across North Africa and the Middle East.
Libyan production outages tightened supply expectations in light sweet crude markets.
OPEC maintained output despite falling prices, accelerating the 2014 to 2015 oil market slide.
OPEC and partners announced production cuts to stabilize the market after prolonged weakness.
Sanctions constrained Iranian oil exports and altered supply expectations.
OPEC+ failed to agree on cuts, triggering a price war and sharp market selloff.
Pandemic lockdowns and storage stress drove extreme dislocations across global oil markets.
The Omicron variant renewed concerns about travel restrictions and weaker oil demand.
The invasion disrupted energy trade expectations and sharply raised geopolitical risk premia.
